title: Thinking in CSS Grid
excerpt: Rows and columns give you a layout language flexbox can't: CSS Grid lets you place content by its position on a two-dimensional plane instead of just along one axis.
body: Flexbox is brilliant for laying things out along a single direction — a row of nav links, a column of form fields. But the moment you need to control rows and columns at the same time, flexbox starts fighting you. That's the gap CSS Grid fills.

With grid-template-columns and grid-template-areas, you describe the shape of a layout directly: a sidebar, a header that spans the full width, a main content area next to it. The browser handles the arithmetic of sizing tracks so the whole page reads like a blueprint rather than a chain of nested boxes.

The real payoff for teaching shows up at the media query. A three-column grid can collapse to a single column by changing one line — grid-template-columns: 1fr instead of repeat(3, 1fr) — without touching the HTML or the individual item styles at all.

title: Why Flexbox Still Matters
excerpt: Grid gets the spotlight, but flexbox is still the right tool anytime you're arranging items along one axis — and it's what makes a responsive navbar so painless.
body: A navigation bar is the textbook flexbox problem: a logo on one side, a handful of links on the other, all vertically centered no matter how tall any one element gets. display: flex plus justify-content: space-between solves it in two lines.

Flexbox also shines with content whose size you don't control ahead of time — a row of tags, a button group, a set of cards that should wrap gracefully onto a new line on a narrow screen. flex-wrap turns a rigid row into a layout that reflows on its own.
The mental model that helps most: grid is for the page's skeleton, flexbox is for the muscles around each bone. Most real interfaces use both, nested inside each other.

title: Loading Data with the Fetch API
excerpt: fetch() turns a static page into one that can load its own content. This post walks through the request, the JSON response, and rendering it into the DOM.
body: Every post on this page, including this one, was loaded with a single fetch('posts.json') call. fetch returns a promise that resolves to a Response object, and calling .json() on that response returns a second promise that resolves to actual JavaScript data.

The pattern worth memorizing is fetch(url).then(res => res.json()).then(data => { /* use data */ }) — or the same thing written with async/await, which reads top to bottom instead of nesting callbacks.

Error handling matters as much as the happy path: a network failure or a bad status code won't automatically throw, so checking res.ok before trusting the response is what keeps a broken request from silently rendering an empty page.
